difficultyRationale: Platform-estimated: EASY because it tests one concept (the behaviour of Python's built-in list methods) by direct recall, with no computation, well under 1 minute for a prepared student.
stem:
Consider the following Python declarations of two lists.

```python
A=[1,2,3]
B=[4,5,6]
```

Which one of the following statements results in `A=` $[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]$?

solution.quick: `A.extend(B)` adds **each element** of `B` to the end of `A` in place, so `A` becomes `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`. `A.append(B)` would add the whole list `B` as **one** element, giving `[1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6]]`. Lists have no `update` method, and `insert` needs an index as well as a value, so (C) and (D) raise errors. Answer: **(A)**.

steps.title: Recall what each method does on a list
steps.body:
| Method | What it does | Arguments |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `L.extend(iterable)` | adds every item of `iterable` to the end of `L`, one by one | 1 |
| `L.append(x)` | adds the object `x` to the end of `L` as a **single** item | 1 |
| `L.insert(i, x)` | inserts `x` just before position `i` | 2 (index **and** value) |
| `L.update(...)` | **not a list method**; `update` exists on `dict` and `set` | – |

`extend`, `append` and `insert` change the list **in place** and return `None`.

steps.title: Trace option (A): A.extend(B)
steps.body:
`extend` iterates over `B = [4, 5, 6]` and appends each element in turn:

$$
[1,2,3] \xrightarrow{+4} [1,2,3,4] \xrightarrow{+5} [1,2,3,4,5] \xrightarrow{+6} [1,2,3,4,5,6]
$$

After the statement, `A == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` and `len(A) == 6`. This is exactly the required result.

steps.title: Trace option (B): A.append(B)
steps.body:
`append` adds its argument as **one** new element. The argument is the list object `B`, so

```python
A == [1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6]]   # len(A) == 4
```

The last element is itself a list (`A[3] == [4, 5, 6]`), so this is **not** `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`.

steps.title: Options (C) and (D) raise errors
steps.body:
- `A.update(B)` raises `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'update'`. Only dictionaries and sets have `update`.
- `A.insert(B)` raises `TypeError: insert expected 2 arguments, got 1`. `insert` needs a position and a value, e.g. `A.insert(3, B)`, and even that would nest `B` as one element: `[1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6]]`.

In both cases the call fails, `A` stays `[1, 2, 3]`, and the program stops unless the exception is handled.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: Only `A.extend(B)` leaves `A` equal to `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`. Running all four options in Python confirms this (see the verification code). Answer: **(A)**.

solution.teaching:
**Lists are mutable sequences.** A Python list is an ordered container of *object references*. Its methods change the list in place and return `None`. That is why you write `A.extend(B)` on its own line, not `A = A.extend(B)`, which would set `A` to `None`.

**The ways to grow a list.**

- `A.append(x)` adds **one** item. If `x` is itself a list, you get a nested list: `[1, 2, 3].append([4, 5, 6])` gives `[1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6]]`.
- `A.extend(iterable)` adds the **items** of the iterable one by one. It works with any iterable: `A.extend("ab")` adds `'a'` and `'b'`, and `A.extend(range(2))` adds `0` and `1`.
- `A.insert(i, x)` puts **one** item `x` before index `i`. It always needs both arguments.
- `A += B` behaves like `A.extend(B)`: it mutates `A` in place.
- `A = A + B` builds a **new** list and rebinds the name `A`. The final value is the same, but other names that referred to the old list do not see the change.

**Where does `update` come from?** `dict.update(other)` merges key–value pairs, and `set.update(iterable)` adds elements to a set. Lists have no such method, so calling it raises `AttributeError`. GATE likes to include a method name that belongs to a *different* built-in type as a distractor.

**A quick way to decide between `append` and `extend`:** ask how much the length grows. `append` always grows it by exactly 1. `extend(B)` grows it by `len(B)`. Here the target has length 6 = 3 + 3, so the method must add three elements, which is `extend`.

**Back to the question.** Starting from `A = [1, 2, 3]` and `B = [4, 5, 6]`, only `A.extend(B)` produces the flat list `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`, so the answer is (A).

optionAnalysis.label: A
optionAnalysis.explanation: `extend` appends the elements `4`, `5`, `6` of `B` one at a time, so `A` becomes `[1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]` (length 6).

optionAnalysis.label: B
optionAnalysis.explanation: `append` adds the whole list `B` as a single element, giving the nested list `[1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6]]` of length 4.

optionAnalysis.label: C
optionAnalysis.explanation: Lists have no `update` method (it belongs to `dict` and `set`), so the call raises `AttributeError` and `A` is unchanged.

optionAnalysis.label: D
optionAnalysis.explanation: `insert` needs two arguments, a position and a value. `A.insert(B)` raises `TypeError: insert expected 2 arguments, got 1`. Even with an index, it would insert `B` as one nested element.

solution.shortcut: The length must grow from 3 to 6. `append` and `insert` add exactly one element, and `update` does not exist for lists. Only `extend` adds `len(B) = 3` elements.
solution.commonTrap: Choosing `A.append(B)` in the belief that it joins two lists. `append` nests `B` as a single element, `[1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6]]`. Another slip is to carry over `update` from sets or dictionaries, where `s.update(B)` does add all the elements, but lists do not have this method.

answerVerification.notes: Independent solve: list.extend adds each element of B in place, so A.extend(B) gives [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; append nests B as one element; lists have no update method; insert requires an index and a value. This gives (A), matching the official key A. The Python check (run on Python 3.11) executes each option on fresh copies of A and B: (A) gives [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]; (B) gives [1, 2, 3, [4, 5, 6]]; (C) raises AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'update'; (D) raises TypeError: insert expected 2 arguments, got 1.
